content.rendered:
It is ironic that the political elite of Northern Nigeria, the region whose citizens are mainly responsible for the terrorism that could engulf the entire Nigeria, is not accepting responsibility for this scourge that is so obvious.

As the sitting Governor of Katsina State, Bello Masari, observed, whereas Northern Nigerians were mostly the top military brass of former President Muhammadu Buhari’s government, the predators and the victims were also Northerners, or from the Sahel.

Prof. Yusuf Usman, a buddy of Sheikh Ahmad Gumi, who appears to be an apologist for terrorists, also observed that, though President Bola Tinubu is currently the Commander-in-Chief of Nigeria’s Armed Forces, the National Security Adviser, the two Ministers of Defence, and many other senior security chiefs are Northerners.

He, therefore, suggested that the Northern elite must also accept responsibility for ending the insecurity, even as it must be acknowledged that the buck stops on the table of the Commander-in-Chief, and all security chiefs, regardless of their region.

When Obafemi Awolowo, the first Premier of Western Nigeria, pointed out that the children that Northern Nigeria failed to educate would turn around to torment their children, he was rebuffed. Now the menace has been unleashed on the whole of Nigeria.

Some observers, who seem to be possessed of extremely grand imagination, suggest that the ultimate agenda of some members of Northern Nigeria’s political establishment is to impose Islam throughout Nigeria, not only to serve their religious preferences, but also their hegemonic hold on the politics and economy of Nigeria.

They argue that, probably after Southern Nigeria rejected President Buhari’s RUGA solution to end herder-farmer clashes, which they suggest was to have been a decoy or Forward Operational Base for a future invasion of Southern Nigeria, the option of direct attack, through kidnapping and bomb blasts, has now been adopted.

That, the argument goes, is why members of the Northern Nigerian political establishment, within or outside government, appear to have a benign, if not exactly indulgent, attitude to the issue of terrorism, even in Northern Nigeria.

There is another conspiracy theory, which suggests that the terrorists are some kind of advance party to expel indigenes of communities whose lands are rich with large deposits of lithium, gold and other valuable mineral resources, ahead of the “invasion” of multinational mining corporations.

They argue that it is not a coincidence that the communities with these mineral resources are usually the operational theatres of the terrorists, who are “hired” to scare the people away for the large-scale, but clandestine, industrial mining of the resources. Well.

That, some of the more imaginative conspiracy theorists say, explains the occasional and “invisible” flights and remote landings of strange aircraft.

One of these landings took place on a road that the Federal Government is still constructing in Delta State, instead of Asaba International Airport, or even the privately operated Osubi Airport.

And indeed, to date, not much information has been released about the isolated flight, after identifying the pilot as an old, possibly confused, man who has gone past the statutory 65 years of age for international and most domestic flights.

Though someone took the photograph of the aircraft, he or she didn’t seem to have had the presence of mind to take (or publish) that of the crew and the passengers. Of course, there were speculations that the aircraft came from Turkiye, recently rumoured, but not confirmed, to be linked to terrorism financing in Nigeria.

But when you counter this suggestion with the argument that terrorists do not seem to operate in the oil fields of the Niger Delta, they argue that the International Oil Corporations are already sitting pretty, ensconced, in the commanding heights of Nigeria’s oil sector.

When Lasisi Olagunju, ace columnist with Nigerian Tribune newspaper, tried to count the fingers of a man with nine fingers, he got an unexpected, but swift, rebuff, surprisingly from retired military Generals of Northern Nigerian origin. He had suggested that the blame for terrorism should be placed at the doorstep of the Northern Nigerian elite.

Olagunju suggested that “Northern Nigeria has, for decades, incubated much of the violence, extremism and instability that continue to threaten national cohesion, yet public discourse by our elders often avoids naming this reality directly.”

While President Buhari was resident in Aso Rock, it was nearly an article of faith to avoid mentioning the ethnic identity of most of those who were involved in the marauding and violent acts against the Nigerian citizens. The one-sided acts of violence were cleverly framed as herder-farmer clashes.

Olagunju added that “Until we are willing to define the problem honestly and acknowledge the (Northern) region’s central role in the crisis, meaningful solutions will be elusive.” One could say, in a manner of speaking, that the hitherto regional malaise has now become a pandemic.

It is surprising, even scary, that a group of retired military generals (and an ambassador), who are friends of Major General Rabe Abubakar, former Director of Army Public Relations, who died in the captivity of terrorists, who abducted him and his wife, could only read a sectional slur to the observations of Olagunju about a national problem.

They arranged a press conference where their spokesman tragically said, “These incidents of insecurity have attracted, not only condemnation, but also taken ethnic colouration, with some commentators blaming the Northern Region for all the ills of the Nigerian state.”

Somehow, this General missed the even more indicting observation by a very concerned and worried Dr Zainab Buhari, a Northern Nigerian, who shot from the hip by indicting the Northern oligarchy with their retrogressive policies of spending millions on mass marriages, which she described as “street kid factory,” (instead of encouraging mass education).

She added, “Terrorism does not start with ideology. It starts with hopelessness… (Terrorists) Do not recruit PhDs. They recruit boys who were ‘produced, but never raised.’” Former First Lady, Patience Jonathan, once described such kids as “Born trowey,” or something like that.

The only way to respond to the officers and gentlemen Generals, who missed the import of the cancerous terrorism that consumed one of their friends, is to quote English poet, Geoffrey Chaucer, who once asked, “If gold rust, what shall iron do? For if a priest (or General?), upon whom we trust (for our security?), be foul, no wonder a layman may yield to lust.” Enough said.

The only way that these Generals can live up to their billing as officers and gentlemen is to respond with more concern over the situation that Nigeria has found itself in, and take a lead in the Northern Nigerian elite’s obligation to accept responsibility for the terrorism and find solutions to it, for the sake of Northern Nigeria and the rest of Nigeria.

If the North, led by these Generals, join the President to end the tragedy, which has become a verb, it will save Nigeria from losing more lives and wasting more money that should be spent on development programmes and projects.

The following words of Senator Shehu Sani should speak to these Generals: “I want to see a common resolve, a common action, a united country, irrespective of your religious affiliation and cultural identity. Rally round our security forces to achieve their ultimate aim of destroying terrorists and their bases in Northern Nigeria.”
